stimuli.text: Initial-rate data for A + B → products:
A student heats 11.9 g of $$\ce{CaCO3(s)}$$, which decomposes completely: $$\ce{CaCO3(s) -> CaO(s) + CO2(g)}$$. The $$\ce{CO2}$$ is collected at 294 K and 0.96 atm.
The decomposition of compound X was monitored at constant temperature.
A student titrates 27.0 mL of 0.16 M weak monoprotic acid HA (Ka = 6.3 \times 10^{-5}) with 0.11 M NaOH.
3 g of $$\ce{NH4NO3}$$ dissolves in 76 g of water in a coffee-cup calorimeter. The temperature falls by 5.5 °C. Assume the solution's specific heat is 4.18 J/(g·°C).

A galvanic cell is made of a Mg electrode in 1.0 M $$\ce{Mg^{2+}}$$ and a Pb electrode in 1.0 M $$\ce{Pb^{2+}}$$. Standard reduction potentials: $$\ce{Mg^{2+} + 2e- -> Mg}$$ E° = -2.37 V; $$\ce{Pb^{2+} + 2e- -> Pb}$$ E° = -0.13 V.
The photoelectron spectra of N (Z = 7) and O (Z = 8) are compared.

questions.stem: A reaction has a theoretical yield of 28.2 g. The actual yield is 19.7 g. What is the percent yield?
What is the pH of a 0.005 M solution of $$\ce{Ca(OH)2}$$ at 25 °C?

options.why: That is the pOH; subtract from 14.
Each formula unit releases two OH⁻.
Strong acids and bases ionize completely; no equilibrium is needed.
Correct. Strong base: [OH⁻] = 2 × 0.005 M; pH = 14 − pOH.

questions.stem: In HCO₃⁻ + H₂O ⇌ CO₃²⁻ + H₃O⁺, which species is the Brønsted–Lowry base?
On a reaction energy profile, the reactants are at 103 kJ/mol, the transition state at 227 kJ/mol and the products at 131 kJ/mol. What is the activation energy of the reverse reaction?

options.why: Correct. Reverse Ea = transition state − products.
Measure from the correct starting point.

questions.explanation: Forward Ea = 124, ΔH = 28, reverse Ea = 96 kJ/mol.

questions.stem: Which intermolecular force is present in all molecules?

options.why: Requires H bonded to N, O or F.
Correct. They arise from temporary dipoles in every electron cloud.

questions.explanation: They arise from temporary dipoles in every electron cloud.

questions.stem: How many moles are in 37 g of $$\ce{Al2O3}$$?

options.why: Correct. n = m/M with M = 102 g/mol.

questions.stem: A reaction has a theoretical yield of 27.8 g. The actual yield is 18.6 g. What is the percent yield?
A mass spectrum of a sample of lithium shows two peaks: mass 6 with relative abundance 84% and mass 7 with 16%. What is the average atomic mass of the sample?

options.why: The isotopes are not equally abundant.
Correct. Weight each isotope mass by its fractional abundance.
Pair each mass with its own abundance.

questions.stem: A gas mixture contains 0.2 mol N₂, 0.6 mol O₂ and 0.7 mol Ar at a total pressure of 1.5 atm. What is the partial pressure of N₂?

options.why: The gases are not present in equal amounts.
Use the mole fraction, not moles.

questions.stem: A 20.9 mL sample of $$\ce{H2SO4}$$ is titrated to the equivalence point with 37.2 mL of 0.18 M NaOH. What is the concentration of the acid?

options.why: Correct. Each H₂SO₄ reacts with two OH⁻, so divide the moles of NaOH by 2.

questions.stem: For $$\ce{A(g) + B(g) <=> 2C(g)}$$, K = 6.7. A mixture has [A] = 0.3 M, [B] = 0.5 M and [C] = 0.6 M. In which direction will the reaction proceed?

options.text: It proceeds in reverse, toward reactants, because Q = 2.4
options.why: If Q is less than K, the reaction proceeds forward.

options.text: It proceeds forward, toward products, because Q = 2.4
options.why: Correct. Q = [C]²/([A][B]) = 2.4, which is less than K.

options.text: It proceeds forward, toward products, because Q = 4
It is at equilibrium, because Q = K

questions.stem: What is the energy of a photon with a wavelength of 611 nm?

options.why: Correct. E = hc/λ, with λ in meters.

questions.stem: How many valence electrons are shown in the Lewis structure of $$\ce{NH4+}$$?

options.why: Correct. Sum the valence electrons of all atoms, then add one per negative charge (subtract one per positive charge).

questions.stem: Steel is harder than pure iron because:

options.text: Small carbon atoms in the gaps (interstitial alloy) hinder layers of iron atoms from sliding
Carbon replaces iron atoms of the same size

questions.stem: A weak acid HA has pKa = 6. In a solution at pH 8.2, which statement is correct?

options.why: Correct. Above the pKa, the deprotonated form dominates.

questions.stem: A weak acid HA has pKa = 4.9. In a solution at pH 4, which statement is correct?

options.why: Correct. Below the pKa, the protonated form dominates.

questions.stem: What is the oxidation number of P in $$\ce{PO4^{3-}}$$?

options.why: Make the oxidation numbers add up to the overall charge.
Make the oxidation numbers add up to the overall charge.
Make the oxidation numbers add up to the overall charge.
Correct. The oxidation numbers must sum to the species' overall charge (O usually −2, H usually +1).

questions.stem: What is the mass percent of Fe in $$\ce{Fe2O3}$$?

options.why: There are 2 atoms of Fe in the formula.
Use masses, not numbers of atoms.
That is the percent of the other elements.

questions.stem: Is $$\ce{CCl4}$$ polar or nonpolar, and why?

options.text: Nonpolar, because its bond dipoles cancel by symmetry
Polar, because its bond dipoles do not cancel
options.why: Consider the molecule's shape, not only its bonds.
Containing H does not make a molecule polar.

options.text: Polar, because all its bonds are polar
options.why: Polarity depends on both bond polarity and geometry.

questions.explanation: CCl4 is tetrahedral; the dipoles cancel.

questions.stem: Which compound has the greater lattice energy, $$\ce{MgF2}$$ or $$\ce{NaCl}$$?

options.text: $$\ce{NaCl}$$, because its ions have larger charges
$$\ce{NaCl}$$, because it has more atoms per formula unit
options.why: Number of atoms does not determine lattice energy.

options.text: $$\ce{MgF2}$$, because its ions have larger charges
options.why: Correct. By Coulomb's law, attraction increases with the product of the ion charges.

options.text: They are equal because both are ionic

questions.explanation: MgF2 has ion charges 2 and 1; NaCl has 1 and 1.

questions.stem: A reaction has K = 16. What is K for the reaction reversed and multiplied by 2?

options.why: Multiplying by n raises K to the nth power.
Correct. Reverse → 1/K; multiply by n → Kⁿ.
K is raised to a power, not multiplied.

questions.stem: 28 mL of 2.2 M solution is diluted to 148 mL. What is the new concentration?

options.why: V₂ is the total final volume.

questions.stem: On a reaction energy profile, the reactants are at 88 kJ/mol, the transition state at 222 kJ/mol and the products at 5 kJ/mol. What is the activation energy of the reverse reaction?

options.why: Correct. Reverse Ea = transition state − products.
Measure from the correct starting point.

questions.explanation: Forward Ea = 134, ΔH = -83, reverse Ea = 217 kJ/mol.

questions.stem: Which is the ground-state electron configuration of chlorine (Cl, Z = 17)?

options.why: Correct. Fill orbitals in order until 17 electrons are placed.

questions.stem: Adding an inert gas to a reaction mixture at constant volume does what to the equilibrium?

options.text: Nothing; partial pressures of the reacting gases are unchanged
Shifts it toward more gas moles
Shifts it toward fewer gas moles

questions.stem: A solution has an absorbance of 1.23 in a 2 cm cuvette. The molar absorptivity is 880 M⁻¹cm⁻¹. What is the concentration?
In a Zn/Cu galvanic cell, [Zn²⁺] is increased. What happens to the cell potential?

options.why: Correct. A product's concentration rises, so Q increases.

questions.explanation: A product's concentration rises, so Q increases.

questions.stem: How can an unfavorable reaction (ΔG positive) be made to occur?

options.text: By coupling it to a favorable reaction so the total ΔG is negative

questions.stem: For $$\ce{N2 + 3H2 -> 2NH3}$$, $$\ce{H2}$$ is consumed at 0.53 M/s. At what rate does $$\ce{NH3}$$ form?

options.why: Correct. Multiply by the coefficient ratio 2/3.
Divide by the reactant's coefficient too.

questions.stem: What is the energy of a photon with a wavelength of 525 nm?

options.why: Correct. E = hc/λ, with λ in meters.

questions.stem: Samples of $$\ce{CO2}$$, $$\ce{H2}$$, $$\ce{N2}$$, $$\ce{Ar}$$ are all at the same temperature. Which has the highest average molecular speed?

options.why: N2 has a larger molar mass (28 g/mol).
Ar has a larger molar mass (40 g/mol).
Correct. At the same temperature, average kinetic energy is equal, so the lightest gas moves fastest.
CO2 has a larger molar mass (44 g/mol).

questions.explanation: Molar masses: CO2 44, H2 2.02, N2 28, Ar 40.

questions.stem: For $$\ce{A(g) + B(g) <=> 2C(g)}$$, K = 7.7. A mixture has [A] = 0.4 M, [B] = 0.1 M and [C] = 0.3 M. In which direction will the reaction proceed?

options.text: It is at equilibrium, because Q = K
It proceeds forward, toward products, because Q = 7.5
It proceeds in reverse, toward reactants, because Q = 2.25
options.why: If Q is less than K, the reaction proceeds forward.

options.text: It proceeds forward, toward products, because Q = 2.25
options.why: Correct. Q = [C]²/([A][B]) = 2.25, which is less than K.

questions.stem: A gas mixture contains 0.7 mol N₂, 0.7 mol O₂ and 0.8 mol Ar at a total pressure of 3.7 atm. What is the partial pressure of N₂?

options.why: The gases are not present in equal amounts.
Use the mole fraction, not moles.

questions.stem: A gas mixture contains 0.9 mol N₂, 0.1 mol O₂ and 0.8 mol Ar at a total pressure of 4.7 atm. What is the partial pressure of N₂?

options.why: Use the mole fraction, not moles.
The gases are not present in equal amounts.

questions.stem: Why is HI a stronger acid than HF?

options.text: The H–I bond is weaker and I⁻ is larger, so H⁺ is released more easily
options.why: Correct. Bond strength decreases down the group.

options.text: F is less electronegative than I

questions.explanation: Bond strength decreases down the group.

questions.stem: Which bond is the most polar?

options.why: Correct. It has the largest electronegativity difference (1.8).

questions.stem: Mechanism: (1) NO₂ + NO₂ → NO₃ + NO (slow); (2) NO₃ + CO → NO₂ + CO₂ (fast). Which rate law is consistent with it?

options.why: Correct. The slow first step determines the rate.
CO is not in the slow step.
That is the overall equation, not the slow step.

questions.explanation: The slow first step determines the rate.

questions.stem: What is the pressure of 0.16 mol of gas in a 17 L container at 410 K?

options.why: With L and atm, use R = 0.08206.

questions.stem: A compound (hydrogen peroxide) is 5.93% H, 94.1% O by mass. What is its empirical formula?

options.why: That is the molecular formula; reduce to the simplest ratio.
Correct. Convert each percent (in 100 g) to moles and divide by the smallest.

questions.explanation: The mole ratio reduces to HO; the molecular formula is H2O2.

questions.stem: Samples of $$\ce{Cl2}$$, $$\ce{CH4}$$, $$\ce{CO2}$$, $$\ce{N2}$$ are all at the same temperature. Which has the highest average molecular speed?

options.why: Cl2 has a larger molar mass (70.9 g/mol).
CO2 has a larger molar mass (44 g/mol).
N2 has a larger molar mass (28 g/mol).
Correct. At the same temperature, average kinetic energy is equal, so the lightest gas moves fastest.

questions.explanation: Molar masses: Cl2 70.9, CH4 16, CO2 44, N2 28.

questions.stem: Why does temperature remain constant while ice melts?

options.text: Covalent bonds in water are breaking
options.why: Melting does not break covalent bonds.

options.text: Added energy overcomes intermolecular forces rather than increasing kinetic energy
options.why: Correct. Phase changes occur at constant temperature.

questions.explanation: Phase changes occur at constant temperature.

questions.stem: 59 g of water at 59 °C is mixed with 172 g of water at 22 °C in an insulated container. What is the final temperature?

options.why: Pair each mass with its own temperature.
Correct. Heat lost = heat gained; for water alone, a mass-weighted average.

questions.stem: A first-order reaction has a rate constant of 0.0495 min⁻¹. What is its half-life?
For $$\ce{N2 + 3H2 -> 2NH3}$$, 50 g of $$\ce{N2}$$ reacts with 88 g of $$\ce{H2}$$. What mass of $$\ce{NH3}$$ can form?

options.why: Not all of both reactants reacts.
Apply the mole ratio from the equation.
Correct. N2 is the limiting reactant.
Use the limiting reactant, which gives less product.

questions.stem: When a reaction involving 0.02 mol of limiting reactant occurs in 148 g of solution (c = 4.18 J/(g·°C)), the temperature rises by 6.5 °C. What is ΔH for the reaction?

options.why: Correct. q(solution) = mcΔT = 4020 J; q(reaction) = −q(solution); divide by moles.
Divide by the moles of reactant.
A temperature rise means the reaction is exothermic (negative ΔH).

questions.stem: What is the pH of a 0.2 M solution of hypochlorous acid (Ka = 3 \times 10^{-8})?

options.why: A weak acid does not ionize completely.
Correct. Solve Ka = x²/(C − x) for x = [H₃O⁺].

questions.stem: What is the rate law?

options.why: Correct. Doubling [A] multiplies the rate by 4; doubling [B] multiplies it by 1.
Orders are found from the data, not from coefficients.
Recheck how the rate changes when [B] doubles.
Compare trials where only one concentration changes.

questions.explanation: Trials 1→2: rate ×4, so order 2 in A. Trials 1→3: rate ×1, so order 0 in B.

questions.stem: What is the pH of a 0.1 M solution of hydrofluoric acid (Ka = 6.8 \times 10^{-4})?

options.why: Correct. Solve Ka = x²/(C − x) for x = [H₃O⁺].
A weak acid does not ionize completely.

questions.stem: In paper chromatography with a nonpolar solvent, which component travels farthest?

options.why: Polar components stay with the polar paper.
Correct. It is most attracted to the nonpolar mobile phase.

questions.explanation: It is most attracted to the nonpolar mobile phase.

questions.stem: What is E°cell for a galvanic cell made from these half-cells?

options.why: E° does not change when half-reactions are multiplied.
Cathode minus anode; a galvanic cell is positive.

questions.stem: At 298 K, ΔG° for a reaction is 11 kJ/mol. What is K?

options.why: Correct. K = e^(−ΔG°/RT), with ΔG° in J/mol and R = 8.314.

questions.explanation: ln K = -4.44; K = 0.0118. Positive ΔG°: K less than 1.

questions.stem: A buffer contains 0.3 mol of a weak acid HA (pKa 4.74) and 0.34 mol of A⁻. What is its pH?
The Ksp of $$\ce{PbI2}$$ is 7.1 \times 10^{-9}. What is its molar solubility in pure water?
10 mL of 0.11 M weak acid HA is titrated with 0.28 M NaOH. What volume of NaOH reaches the equivalence point?

options.why: Correct. Moles of base = moles of acid.

questions.stem: Reaction 1 has ΔH₁ = -290 kJ and reaction 2 has ΔH₂ = -344 kJ. A target reaction is obtained by doubling reaction 1 and adding reaction 2. What is ΔH for the target reaction?

options.why: Reversing changes the sign of ΔH₂.
Enthalpies add; they do not multiply.
Correct. Reverse → change sign; multiply → multiply ΔH; then add.

questions.stem: The first four ionization energies of an element are 518, 3626, 5657, 8316 kJ/mol. In which group of the periodic table is the element most likely found?

options.why: Locate the largest jump between successive ionization energies.
Locate the largest jump between successive ionization energies.
Locate the largest jump between successive ionization energies.
Correct. The large jump comes after removing 1 electron, so it has 1 valence electron.

questions.explanation: The big jump marks the start of removing core electrons.

questions.stem: Calculate ΔH° for $$\ce{C2H5OH + 3O2 -> 2CO2 + 3H2O(l)}$$. (ΔH°f of O₂ is 0.)

options.why: Correct. Σ n ΔH°f(products) − Σ n ΔH°f(reactants).
Multiply each ΔH°f by its coefficient.

questions.stem: For $$\ce{H2(g) + I2(g) <=> 2HI(g)}$$, initial [H₂] = 0.5 M and [I₂] = 1.5 M, with no HI. At equilibrium, [HI] = 0.42 M. What is K?
Use the bond enthalpies to estimate ΔH for $$\ce{CH4 + 2O2 -> CO2 + 2H2O}$$.

options.why: Broken minus formed, not formed minus broken.
Bonds formed release energy: subtract them.
Multiply each bond energy by the number of bonds.
Correct. ΔH ≈ Σ(bonds broken) − Σ(bonds formed).

questions.stem: For a reaction, ΔH° = 41 kJ/mol and ΔS° = 181 J/(mol·K). What is ΔG° at 463 K, and is the reaction favorable?

options.why: Convert ΔS from J to kJ.
Correct. ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, with ΔS in kJ/(mol·K).

parts.prompt: Calculate the number of moles of CO₂ produced.

rubric.criterion: Correct moles using molar mass 100.09 g/mol and the 1:1 ratio.

parts.prompt: Calculate the volume of CO₂ expected.
The student measures 2.898 L of gas. Calculate the percent yield, and give one experimental reason the yield could be less than 100%.

rubric.example: Incomplete decomposition (not heated long enough) or gas leaking from the apparatus.

parts.prompt: Draw (describe) a complete Lewis diagram for CO₂, and identify its molecular geometry and the hybridization of carbon.

rubric.example: O=C=O with two lone pairs on each O (16 valence electrons).

parts.prompt: Explain why CO₂ is nonpolar even though C=O bonds are polar.

rubric.criterion: Linear symmetry makes the bond dipoles cancel.

parts.prompt: CaO is an ionic solid. Explain, using Coulomb's law, why CaO has a higher melting point than KCl.

rubric.criterion: Larger ion charges in CaO (2+/2−) than in KCl (1+/1−).
Greater electrostatic attraction (and smaller ions) means more energy is needed to separate the ions.

parts.prompt: Calculate the average rate of disappearance of X between 0 and 20 s.
Determine the order of the reaction with respect to X. Justify your answer using the data.

rubric.example: Equal time intervals give equal changes in 1/[X].

parts.prompt: Write the rate law and determine the rate constant, with units.
Calculate the half-life of the reaction (for the initial concentration).
A proposed mechanism has a slow first step: 2X → X₂. Is the mechanism consistent with the rate law? Explain.

rubric.criterion: Yes; the slow step's elementary rate law matches the observed rate law.

parts.prompt: A catalyst is added. Explain its effect on the rate and on the rate constant, using activation energy.

rubric.example: The catalyst provides a new pathway.

rubric.criterion: Lower activation energy means a larger fraction of collisions are successful.

parts.prompt: Write the net ionic equation for the titration reaction.
Calculate the initial pH of the acid solution.

rubric.criterion: Ka expression set up with x = [H₃O⁺].

parts.prompt: Calculate the volume of NaOH needed to reach the equivalence point.
What is the pH at the half-equivalence point? Justify.
Calculate the pH at the equivalence point.

rubric.criterion: Uses Kb = Kw/Ka and the diluted [A⁻].

parts.prompt: Choose an appropriate indicator from: methyl orange (pKa 3.7), bromothymol blue (pKa 7.0), phenolphthalein (pKa 9.3). Justify.

rubric.criterion: Indicator whose pKa is closest to the equivalence pH.

parts.prompt: Explain why the solution at the half-equivalence point resists pH change when a small amount of HCl is added.

rubric.criterion: A⁻ reacts with added H⁺ to form HA (buffer).
rubric.example: A⁻ + H₃O⁺ → HA + H₂O, so the ratio [A⁻]/[HA] changes only slightly.

parts.prompt: Is the dissolution endothermic or exothermic? Justify.

rubric.example: Endothermic: the solution cooled, so energy was absorbed.

parts.prompt: Calculate the heat absorbed or released by the solution.
Calculate ΔH of dissolution in kJ/mol.
If some heat escaped to the surroundings, would the magnitude of the calculated ΔH be too large or too small? Explain.

rubric.criterion: Too small, because the measured temperature change is smaller than the true change.

parts.prompt: Write the balanced net ionic equation for the cell reaction.
Calculate E°cell.
Calculate ΔG° for the cell reaction.
The concentration of Mg²⁺ is increased to 2.0 M. Predict the effect on the cell potential and justify.

rubric.criterion: E decreases because Q increases (a product's concentration rises).
rubric.example: Q greater than 1 → E less than E°.

questions.title: Solubility of a slightly soluble salt

parts.prompt: Write the Ksp expression.
Calculate the molar solubility in pure water.
Calculate the molar solubility in a solution containing 0.1 M OH⁻ (from a soluble salt).
Explain how lowering the pH affects the solubility.

rubric.criterion: Correct reasoning about whether the anion is basic.
rubric.example: Solubility increases: H⁺ reacts with OH⁻ (a base), shifting the equilibrium toward dissolving.

parts.prompt: Write the electron configuration of O.
Explain why the 1s peak of O has a higher binding energy than the 1s peak of N.

rubric.criterion: O has more protons, so 1s electrons are attracted more strongly (Coulomb's law).

parts.prompt: Describe one difference in the number or relative height of peaks between the two spectra.

rubric.criterion: A valid difference based on configurations.
rubric.example: O has one more electron, so its outermost peak is taller or an extra peak appears.

parts.prompt: Which element has the larger atomic radius? Justify using Coulomb's law.

rubric.criterion: N: fewer protons with similar shielding, so valence electrons are held less tightly.
rubric.example: Same period; effective nuclear charge increases across.
